final_qi.question: Is Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, a syndrome that has only been observed in very few cases, associated with a condition in which one or more of the phalanges of the fingers and toes are smaller than normal?
final_qi.long_answer: Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_3], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_5]. Detailed explanation: The question asks if there is an association between Berk–Tabatznik syndrome and a condition characterized by smaller phalanges. The provided context states that Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with symptoms that include brachytelephalangy, which refers to abnormally short (or smaller) phalanges. Since this specific phenotype is clearly mentioned in the context, the answer is 'yes'.

section: introduction
heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] as of july 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include holt–oram syndrome, berk–tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, slovenian type and heart-hand syndrome, spanish type.[5]
section: types
heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as holt–oram syndrome. is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] it is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. the syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as berk–tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] berk–tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. this condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a spanish family. it is also known as heart-hand syndrome, spanish type.[8][9] heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a spanish family. it is also known as heart-hand syndrome, spanish type.[8][9] several people in multiple generations have had this type. it causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] described in one family. a unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] described in one family. a unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] it has been confirmed that patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of char syndrome. hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

llm.short_answer: Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a rare heart-hand syndrome characterized by short stature, congenital optic atrophy, and brachytelephalangy.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_2], [GG_5], [GG_8], [GG_15], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_3]. Detailed explanation: Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, also known as heart-hand syndrome type 2, is an extremely rare condition of unknown cause. It is primarily characterized by short stature, congenital optic atrophy, and brachytelephalangy. Some references additionally note features such as a cleft nare and brachydactyly, further indicating limb anomalies associated with the condition.

Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

llm.short_answer: A rare heart-hand syndrome characterized by short stature, congenital optic atrophy, and brachytelephalangy.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_3]. Detailed explanation: Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, which is also known as heart-hand syndrome type 2, is a condition of unknown cause that exhibits distinct characteristics including short stature, congenital optic atrophy, and brachytelephalangy. This syndrome is extremely rare, with only two cases described.

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1] - Information about: Heart-hand syndromes - berk–tabatznik syndrome
Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1] - Information about: Heart-hand syndromes - berk–tabatznik syndrome
Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

The context describing Berk–Tabatznik syndrome clearly states that it is associated with brachytelephalangy, which refers to shortening (or smaller size) of the phalanges. Since brachytelephalangy is the defining descriptor of 'smaller phalanges,' the context explicitly supports that there is an association.

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

llm.long_answer: Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1], [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_3]. Detailed explanation: The provided context explicitly describes Berk–Tabatznik syndrome as heart‐hand syndrome type 2. It is characterized by short stature, congenital optic atrophy, and brachytelephalangy – a term that refers to abnormally small or shortened (smaller) phalanges. Thus, the context directly supports an association between Berk–Tabatznik syndrome and the condition characterized by smaller phalanges.

Brachytelephalangy refers to abnormally short (or smaller) phalanges. Therefore, the context explicitly supports an association between Berk–Tabatznik syndrome and the condition characterized by smaller phalanges.

Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1] - Information about: Heart-hand syndromes - berk–tabatznik syndrome
Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1] - Information about: Heart-hand syndromes - berk–tabatznik syndrome
Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]

- Reference: [CRAWL_NER_WIKI_1] - Information about: Heart-hand syndromes - berk–tabatznik syndrome
Section: Introduction
Heart-hand syndromes are a group of rare diseases that manifest with both heart and limb deformities.[1][2][3][4] As of July 2013[update], known heart-hand syndromes include Holt–Oram syndrome, Berk–Tabatznik syndrome, brachydactyly-long thumb syndrome, patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome, heart hand syndrome, Slovenian type and Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[5]
Section: Types
Heart-hand syndrome type 1 is more commonly known as Holt–Oram syndrome. Is the most prevalent form of heart-hand syndrome.[1] It is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects bones in the arms and hands (the upper limbs) and may also cause heart problems. The syndrome includes an absent radial bone in the arms, an atrial septal defect, and a first degree heart block.[6] Heart-hand syndrome type 2 is also known as Berk–Tabatznik syndrome.[citation needed] Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is a condition with an unknown cause that shows symptoms of short stature, congenital optic atrophy and brachytelephalangy. This condition is extremely rare with only two cases being found.[7] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Heart-hand syndrome type 3 is very rare and has been described only in three members of a Spanish family. It is also known as Heart-hand syndrome, Spanish type.[8][9] Several people in multiple generations have had this type. It causes sudden cardiac death due to ventricular tachycardia, and it prominently causes a unique type of brachydactyly with mild hand involvement and more severe foot involvement.[10] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] Described in one family. A unique feature in the syndrome is symmetric brachydactyly with long thumbs.[11] It has been confirmed that Patent ductus arteriosus-bicuspid aortic valve syndrome is a distinct syndrome from an allelic variant of Char syndrome. Hand anomalies include metacarpal hypoplasia.[12]
